meta.title: Who really said "With great power comes great responsibility"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Voltaire. No such line exists in his works. The idea traces to an anonymous 1793 French decree, and the modern wording was popularized by Spider-Man in 1962.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'With great power comes great responsibility'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Voltaire. The earliest documented match is an anonymous 1793 French National Convention decree; the modern wording comes from a 1962 Spider-Man comic.

answer.label: Not Voltaire — a proverb popularized by Spider-Man
answer.sourceLine: The Voltaire credit is unsupported — no such line appears anywhere in his works. The closest documented ancestor is an anonymous French National Convention decree of 8 May 1793, and the familiar English wording was popularized by a caption in Marvel’s ‘Amazing Fantasy’ #15 (1962): “with great power there must also come—great responsibility!”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: And a lean, silent figure slowly fades in the gathering darkness, aware at last that in this world, with great power there must also come — great responsibility!
trail: Not in Voltaire. Quote Investigator ↗ reports researchers have been “unable to locate this statement in the oeuvre of Voltaire,” and calls the linkage unsupported.

Earliest documented match, 1793. A French National Convention decree of 8 May 1793 reads “une grande responsabilité est la suite inséparable d’un grand pouvoir” — great responsibility inseparably follows great power (Wikipedia ↗).
The modern wording is Spider-Man’s. Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962) closed with a caption crediting the hero’s new resolve — the line Stan Lee and Steve Ditko sent into pop culture (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The 1962 Spider-Man caption — an omniscient narrator’s line, not spoken by Uncle Ben or Peter Parker. The tighter modern proverb crystallized later.
source.rightsNote: The exact modern proverb is an anonymous crystallization with no single identifiable source work, so no public-domain claim can be made. Its closest documented ancestor — the 1793 French decree — is public domain, but that is different wording; and the popularizing 1962 Amazing Fantasy #15 caption is in copyright to Marvel. Because the exact line’s origin cannot be tied to one work, rights are uncertain.

author.name: Stan Lee & Steve Ditko
author.heading: The real vector
author.metaLine: Amazing Fantasy #15, 1962 · Marvel Comics creators of Spider-Man
author.bio: Writer Stan Lee (1922–2018) and artist Steve Ditko (1927–2018) created Spider-Man for Marvel’s Amazing Fantasy #15 in 1962. The story’s closing narrative caption — not a line of dialogue — carried the moral that hardened over the following decades into the proverb “with great power comes great responsibility.” Quote Investigator names the pair as “important vectors for the popularization of the saying,” though the underlying idea long predates them.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A feel-good, quotable line pinned on a famous Enlightenment name — the classic misattribution pattern. The credit does not survive contact with Voltaire’s actual writings.

items.why: No such statement has been found anywhere in Voltaire’s works. Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikipedia ↗ both describe the Voltaire credit as a misattribution.
The oldest documented version is a French National Convention decree of 8 May 1793; Quote Investigator ascribes the saying to its unknown writer, noting the exact identity is unrecorded (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The exact modern wording comes from Marvel’s Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962), and the earliest documented ancestor is an anonymous 1793 French decree — not Voltaire (Wikipedia ↗).

context.heading: Why the credit is wrong
lead: The thought is old and widely shared — echoes appear in Luke 12:48 (“to whom much is given, much will be required”) and in a string of 19th-century statesmen. But the specific attribution to Voltaire has no textual basis at all.

What makes the line ubiquitous today is Spider-Man. The 1962 caption in Amazing Fantasy #15 fixed the pairing of power and responsibility in the popular mind, and the 2002 film’s Uncle Ben delivered the tightened proverb we now quote.
context.detailsSummary: Other statesmen who said something similar
detailsBody: In 1817 the British MP William Lamb (later Lord Melbourne) argued that “the possession of great power necessarily implies great responsibility” during a habeas corpus debate.
Later figures including Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt used related formulations — evidence the sentiment was a common one, not a single author’s coinage.
